introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá spent most of his life confined to one city, and kept up a correspondence with thousands of people he had never met or would not see again. These hundred passages are taken from that correspondence, and their subject is the correspondence itself: what makes a person present. He tells his friends that remembering is “itself a letter”; that a late answer or a silence of months does not mean they are forgotten; that a thousand leagues do not separate hearts turned toward the same centre; that there is “speech and utterance without lips or tongue”; that he prays for them night and day; and that when they gather he is among them. Paul’s letters from prison are the nearest thing in literature to these, and are quoted often. Seneca, Donne, Shakespeare and Whitman each found words for presence in absence. The doubters are here as well: Arnold, for whom “we mortal millions live alone”; Lamb, whose old familiar faces are simply gone; Tennyson longing for a hand to touch; the proverb that prefers a neighbour near to a brother far; and Hobbes, who asks how one knows that a communication of spirit is more than a dream.
questions: “The very act of remembering and thinking is itself a letter.” Whom did you last remember in that way, and did they come to know it?
Many of these letters begin by excusing a silence. What do they say a silence between friends does and does not mean?
Arnold: “We mortal millions live alone.” Paul: “absent in body, but present in spirit.” Which is nearer to your experience, and what would move you toward the other?
“There is a spiritual language … by which the hearts speak to one another.” When have you understood, or been understood by, someone without words?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá prayed for his correspondents “night and day.” What does praying for an absent friend do for the friendship?
“The real meeting consists in the communication of heart.” What makes a gathering of people who are all in one room a real meeting, on this definition?

outside.why: Friends must “send fragrant messages from one to another.” Proverbs uses the same image: ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man’s friend.
To “receive strength from one another.” Bacon on what happens when a person opens himself to a friend: it redoubleth joys, and cutteth griefs in halfs.

On a wearying journey, the thought of the friends turned pain into ease. Shakespeare’s sonnet ends the same way: but if the while I think on thee, dear friend, all losses are restored and sorrows end.
“Now say whatever your troubled heart desires.” Emerson: a friend is a person with whom I may be sincere. Before him I may think aloud.

“Although in body we are far from one another, yet … with life and heart we are present in one assembly.” Paul to a church he had never visited: though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit.
“That which is in the heart can be neither translated into words nor written on paper.” Tennyson: words, like Nature, half reveal and half conceal the Soul within.
Lovers speak without a word, as clouds speak to the earth and the sun to the eye. The psalm on a speech without sound: there is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard.
Job’s friends, before they spoiled it by talking, sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him.
Remembering is itself a letter; still, “the outward eye and ear” have their claim. Seneca to Lucilius: I never receive a letter from you without being in your company forthwith.
“There is no mightier bond … than the attachment of the heart.” The Song of Songs: many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
“I have not forgotten them for a moment.” Paul from prison: I have you in my heart; God is my record, how greatly I long after you all.

Spiritual communication is “a matter of faith, not based on historical records.” Matthew Arnold could not believe it: in the sea of life enisled, with echoing straits between us thrown, we mortal millions live alone. What experience of yours supports him, and what supports the readings?
A letter rejoiced the heart. Proverbs: as cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
“The bonds of love and heart connection remain firmly linked like a chain.” The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David.
“My heart was uplifted by its contents.” Two disciples, afterwards: did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?
A mere trace, a piece of news, “becomes the illumination of heart and sight.” Proverbs: the light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart: and a good report maketh the bones fat.

Letters are good companions in separation, yet something else consoles more. John closes a short letter: I will not with ink and pen write unto thee: but I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face. What can a letter carry, and what can it not?
That “the sweet fragrances of ancient companionship may reach the hearts … of the friends.” John ends a letter as these letters often end: our friends salute thee. Greet the friends by name.

“The secrets of hearts through written traces.” Emily Dickinson wrote without expecting an answer: this is my letter to the world, that never wrote to me. How is writing to a friend who will reply different from her kind of letter?
“And now again we have thought of thee and set about penning this letter.” Paul, who usually dictated: ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand.
In a letter he had, “like one absent yet present, conversed with you.” Paul’s phrase: absent in body, but present in spirit.
A letter is answered at once, out of love. Paul, on hearing from Thessalonica: ye have good remembrance of us always, desiring greatly to see us, as we also to see you.
“No trace of the pen was manifested,” and yet nothing was forgotten. Isaiah: can a woman forget her sucking child? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.
A delay in letters does no harm; “the inner doors are open.” Seneca: a friend should be retained in the spirit; such a friend can never be absent.
The answer is late, but “my love is constant and permanent for thee.” Shakespeare: love is not love which alters when it alteration finds.
“This separation and remoteness exists in the earthly world, not in the pure soul.” Paul: taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart.

“Lack of news causes intensity of connection.” Proverbs speaks for the one who waits: hope deferred maketh the heart sick. When has silence deepened a friendship of yours, and when has it worn one away?
Between them was a faithful courier, “that reciprocal feeling of heart and conscience.” Proverbs: as in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man.
“Thou hast always been remembered and been present here.” Paul: I thank my God upon every remembrance of you.

No letter was written, yet the correspondence “was uninterrupted.” Charles Lamb knew the other outcome of silence: all, all are gone, the old familiar faces. What kept these friendships from going the way of his?
“Without need for paper and pen, our spiritual communion will be everlasting.” Paul: ye are our epistle written in our hearts, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God.
“When this connection exists, bodily separation is not important.” Donne, leaving on a journey: our two souls endure not yet a breach, but an expansion, like gold to airy thinness beat.
“I am always with you and although I am far from you in body, yet in spirit I am ever near.” Jesus, at parting: lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.
“The Spiritual Breath is a messenger between us.” Proverbs on what a good messenger is worth: as the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to them that send him.

Hidden from sight, yet “visible and manifest” in the world of the heart. Tennyson could not make that exchange: but O for the touch of a vanish’d hand, and the sound of a voice that is still! Do the readings deny this longing or answer it?
“Physical distance has no effect—the far is near and the absent is present.” Whitman to readers not yet born: it avails not, time nor place—distance avails not, I am with you.
Proverbs is more practical: better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off. What can only someone near do for you, and what does that leave for the friend far away?

A hundred thousand leagues, “yet the heart is near … both in the bright day and the dark night.” The psalmist says it of God: if I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me.
Plains, deserts and mountains stand between. Shakespeare: if the dull substance of my flesh were thought, injurious distance should not stop my way.
“The boundless ocean lies between us,” and still they are companions. The parting words at Mizpah: the Lord watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.

Paul’s parting from the elders of Ephesus on the shore shows what such friends feel when the sea is about to lie between them: they all wept sore, sorrowing most of all that they should see his face no more.
A thousand leagues, and “the fragrance of love” still reaches. The Song of Songs: set me as a seal upon thine heart: for love is strong as death.
“Think not that thou art distant and estranged … thou art present in this gathering.” Paul: ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints.
“Nearness is through heart and soul, not through the weak body.” The Qur’án, of the centre that all share: He is with you wheresoever ye may be.
“A companionship that has no separation.” Ruth to Naomi: whither thou goest, I will go; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.
Two brothers of one family may be at odds, while two who are far apart are as brother and sister. Proverbs: there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
An Easterner and a Westerner meet and are at once in fellowship. A disciple of Confucius, to a man who grieved that he had no brothers: all within the four seas will be his brothers.

Political relations “can be disrupted in a single day”; spiritual ones endure. The Qur’án on what makes them: if thou hadst spent all that is in the earth thou couldst not have attuned their hearts, but Allah hath attuned them.
“You are two good sisters.” The first believers in Jerusalem: of one heart and of one soul.
“The essential meeting is that spiritual attachment.” Montaigne, asked why he loved his friend: because it was he, because it was I.
“Each bosom must be a telegraph station.” The first message sent over Morse’s line in 1844 was a verse of Numbers: What hath God wrought.
Thoreau was unimpressed by the wire: our inventions are but improved means to an unimproved end. What must be true of the two people at the ends for any means of communication to matter?
“Speech and utterance without lips or tongue.” Paul: the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
Proverbs sets a limit: the heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy. Is there a part of a person that no friend reaches? What do the readings say reaches it?
“I commune with you through heart and soul.” Pascal: the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
“The Spirit knoweth the spirit, the Spirit addresseth the spirit.” Tennyson: Spirit with Spirit can meet—closer is He than breathing, and nearer than hands and feet.
“The spirit speaks in every language, in no particular tongue.” At Pentecost every man heard them speak in his own language.
“A language by which the hearts speak to one another.” The psalm: deep calleth unto deep.
“Come thou forth that I may hear thy melodies and thou mayest hear Mine.” The Song of Songs: I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh.
To “hear the melodies of God from the Divine Lote-Tree.” Rúmí begins his poem with a listening: hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains, lamenting its banishment from its home.
“My heart leaps within me at your mention.” Paul to Corinth: ye are in our hearts to die and live with you.
He “continually … begs from the Kingdom of Abhá inexhaustible favors for the friends.” Paul: I cease not to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers.
“Night and day I remember thee.” Paul to Timothy: without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day; greatly desiring to see thee.

Day and night occupied with writing, and “longing for the face and presence of the friends.” Paul to Rome: I long to see you, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me.
“Night and day we are not free from mentioning” the friends. Paul’s report of one such friend: always labouring fervently for you in prayers.

No letters for some time, “yet I was always mindful of you and would beseech … confirmation.” Tennyson’s dying Arthur: more things are wrought by prayer than this world dreams of. Wherefore, let thy voice rise like a fountain for me night and day.
“Mine inmost heart is thrilling with the remembrance of the loved ones.” The exiles’ vow: if I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
Burns turned the same vow into a question that answers itself: should auld acquaintance be forgot, and never brought to min’?
A heart stirred “like a fresh sapling … by the breeze of remembrance.” The psalm: when I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches.
A visitor’s arrival is the occasion; the cause was “the stirrings of conscience.” Paul to Philemon: we have great joy and consolation in thy love.

“I am now viewing the flowers in the little garden and remembering thy rose-like face.” Wordsworth: they flash upon that inward eye which is the bliss of solitude; and then my heart with pleasure fills.
“Though I do not see thee with mine eyes, I do see thee with my heart.” Peter: whom having not seen, ye love.
What tie could there be between a prisoner in ‘Akká and a friend far away, unless it were heavenly? Hebrews: remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them.
In prison, “occupied with thy remembrance.” Isaiah: behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands.

The friends are “ever embracing one another, fully conscious and attentive.” Paul: whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.

Kahlil Gibran, on closeness: let there be spaces in your togetherness, and let the winds of the heavens dance between you. The friends in these readings have plenty of space between them. What does distance give a friendship?

“Thou art in India and we are in Syria … yet thou art present in our gathering.” The Prophet: the believers resemble one body, so that, if any part of the body is not well then the whole body shares the sleeplessness and fever with it.

“Your absence is presence.” Shakespeare’s Constance knows an absence that fills a room in another way: grief fills the room up of my absent child, lies in his bed, walks up and down with me. What makes an absent person’s presence a joy, as here, and not a grief?
“Wherever you are, whatever you do … you will be here in spirit.” Paul: always in every prayer of mine for you all making request with joy.

“Whenever an illumined assembly of the friends of God is gathered, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, although bodily absent, is yet present.” Jesus: where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
A gathering held as a “Lord’s Supper” in a home. The first such gatherings: breaking bread from house to house, they did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart.
“When you engage in remembrance … remember this yearning one.” The writer to the Hebrews: pray for us, that I may be restored to you the sooner.
He knows “with absolute certainty that that gathering is illumined.” The Qur’án on who else is in any room: there is no secret conference of three but He is their fourth.
“All the branches of the Blessed Tree are at all times present.” Jesus: I am the vine, ye are the branches.
“Intimacy requires gathering in one region,” yet these friends are near. Thoreau counted what a room is for: I had three chairs in my house; one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society.
Scattered through the world, “spiritually we are gathered in the assembly of fellowship.” Malachi: they that feared the Lord spake often one to another: and a book of remembrance was written.
“Though they are physically far, they are spiritually present in the gathering.” Hebrews, of those who went before: we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses.
Present “in the heavenly gathering.” The Qur’án’s picture of it: as brethren, face to face.

“The heart of man is open to inspiration … As in a dream one talks.” Hobbes: to say he hath spoken to him in a Dream, is no more then to say he dreamed that God spake to him. How would you tell an inspiration from a wish? What tests do the readings imply?
Hearts spiritually related have meetings that “are eternal, both in this world and in the Universe of God.” Paul: neither death, nor life, nor height, nor depth, shall be able to separate us.
“That spirit can communicate with spirit is proven by the known fact of teaching.” Proverbs: iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Photographs pass away; “the true picture” is kept elsewhere. Paul: the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
“He talks with me in midnights. He wakes me in the morning.” The psalmist: when I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches.
“When two hearts are united together astonishing results will be seen.” Ecclesiastes: two are better than one; for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.
“It is Love that establishes communication between the hearts.” John: if we love one another, God dwelleth in us.
Donne on why no one’s joy or loss is private: no man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent.
Pilgrims at the holy Shrine are asked to remember those who could not come. A pilgrim’s psalm: for my brethren and companions’ sakes, I will now say, Peace be within thee.
A neighbour in London is told to “prove and establish your neighborliness before all.” A lawyer’s question, which Jesus answered with a story about what a neighbour does: and who is my neighbour?

Serve so that the spirits of those gone before “may become joyous and glad.” George Eliot on how the dead still act on the living: the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts.
When the friends praise and teach, the Concourse on high takes notice. Jesus: joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth.

philippians-i-have-you-in-my-heart.text: Even as it is meet for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart; inasmuch as both in my bonds, and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, ye all are partakers of my grace. For God is my record, how greatly I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ

romans-without-ceasing-i-make-mention.text: For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I make mention of you always in my prayers; Making request, if by any means now at length I might have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come unto you. For I long to see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual gift, to the end ye may be established; That is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me

timothy-remembrance-of-thee-night-and-da.text: I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day; Greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy

philemon-joy-and-consolation-in-thy-love.text: For we have great joy and consolation in thy love, because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother

seneca-never-receive-a-letter.text: I thank you for writing to me so often; for you are revealing your real self to me in the only way you can. I never receive a letter from you without being in your company forthwith

seneca-friend-retained-in-the-spirit.text: A friend should be retained in the spirit; such a friend can never be absent. He can see every day whomsoever he desires to see
seneca-friend-retained-in-the-spirit.author: Seneca

whitman-distance-avails-not.text: It avails not, time nor place—distance avails not, / I am with you, you men and women of a generation, or ever so many generations hence, / Just as you feel when you look on the river and sky, so I felt
whitman-distance-avails-not.author: Walt Whitman

shakespeare-injurious-distance.text: If the dull substance of my flesh were thought, / Injurious distance should not stop my way; / For then despite of space I would be brought, / From limits far remote, where thou dost stay

lamb-old-familiar-faces.text: I have had playmates, I have had companions, / In my days of childhood, in my joyful school-days, / All, all are gone, the old familiar faces

dickinson-letter-to-the-world.text: This is my letter to the world, / That never wrote to me,— / The simple news that Nature told, / With tender majesty. / Her message is committed / To hands I cannot see; / For love of her, sweet countrymen, / Judge tenderly of me
dickinson-letter-to-the-world.author: Emily Dickinson
